newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish referendum seen no threat to Amsterdam pact.
newsitem.headline: Danish referendum seen no threat to Amsterdam pact.

text.p: When Danes vote in a referendum on the revised European Union treaty now being drafted in Amsterdam there should be little chance of them repeating their 1992 rejection of the Maastricht treaty, analysts here believe.

Economy Minister Marianne Jelved, speaking to Reuters at the start of the two-day Amsterdam summit of EU leaders said on Monday that the final treaty text would most probably require a Danish referendum, possibly in February or March next year.

But the thorniest issues are already covered by exemptions granted to Denmark in 1992, in which it opted out of economic and monetary union -- not part of the treaty revisions -- and joint European defence, policing and asylum policies.
Armed with the exemptions the government called a fresh plebiscite in 1993 in which voters accepted Maastricht on the basis of the waivers.
The opt-outs are expected to be carried foward into the new accord, meaning that related issues need not be put to the vote again.

That leaves relatively unproblematic areas such as initiatives for job creation, environmental standards and protection against discrimination, which Danish leaders should be able to present to voters with no great difficulty.

"This should all be manageable for them. At the end of the day the Danes will come away with their opt-outs preserved, if they do that they won't have to have a referendum on those points so that's bound to help them," a diplomat said.

"I think it all depends a little bit on what emerges (from the summit) at the end of the day, but at the moment it's all looking as if they can present it as (Prime Minister Poul Nyrup) Rasmussen achieving some his objectives," he added.

One drawback might be if the summit, the culmination of 15 months of negotiation known collectively as the inter -governmental conference (IGC), decides that a further round of IGC talks is needed to shape procedural reforms ahead of the admission of new EU members from eastern and central Europe.
Should that occur, Danes who have been told by their politicians that expansion is the top priority of the talks, might feel cheated, some government officials fear.
Rasmussen himself might have tied the issues too closely, when he used the membership issue as an argument for ratifying the new treaty.
"For me, to say no to the Amsterdam accord is to say no to enlargement," he said.
But most treaty-watchers believe that with the key issues of defence and border controls neutralised by the existing opt-outs the most likely response to the remainder will be apathy.
"Eurosceptics are going to find it hard to find issues around which to moblise opposition," a parliamentary researcher said.
"I would be astonished if Rasmussen came back with a package which he couldn't sell," the diplomat said.
